title: Review: Resistivity; Series and parallel circuits; Kirchhoff's laws
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL04-uk1#t2 term and clue written for the game; EL06-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; EL06-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL04-uk1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL04-uk1#N.11, EL06-1#N.10a, EL04-uk1#N.3, EL06-1#N.7, EL04-uk1#N.7, EL06-1#N.2, EL04-uk1#N.10, EL06-1#N.11, EL04-uk1#N.12, EL06-1#N.4. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Crocodile clip
items.clue: Sliding connector that sets the length of wire being tested.

items.label: Ammeter
items.clue: Instrument placed in series; an ideal one has zero resistance.

items.label: Open circuit
items.clue: A gap anywhere in a loop, so that no current flows in that loop.

items.label: Voltmeter
items.clue: Instrument connected across the chosen length of wire, giving V for R = V/I.

questions.stem: A copper wire and a sample of pure silicon, a semiconductor, are both cooled from 20 °C to −20 °C. How does the resistance of each change, and why?

options.text: Copper's falls: less ion vibration. Silicon's rises: fewer charge carriers.
Both fall, as the ions in each vibrate less, so there are fewer collisions.
Copper's falls, as fewer electrons are freed; silicon's rises, as its ions vibrate more.
Both rise, since cooling makes the charge carriers in each move more slowly.

questions.explanation: Right. In copper the carrier number hardly changes, so fewer collisions win. In silicon the carrier number drops sharply, which outweighs the smaller vibration.

questions.stem: A student wants to measure the current in a lamp and the pd across it, but connects the meters the wrong way round. The circuit is: a cell, a voltmeter and the lamp connected in series in a single loop, with an ammeter connected in parallel with the lamp. Both meters are ideal. What does the student observe?

options.text: The lamp is off and both meters read zero, as there is no current in the circuit.
The lamp is off, the ammeter reads zero and the voltmeter reads the emf of the cell.
The ammeter short-circuits the lamp, so a very large current flows through the ammeter.
The lamp lights normally, and the meters show its current and pd as when correctly connected.

questions.stem: A student plots R against length for a uniform wire of diameter 0.40 mm. The best-fit line has a gradient of 4.0 Ω m⁻¹ and crosses the R axis at 0.30 Ω. What is the resistivity of the wire?

options.text: 4.0 Ω m

questions.explanation: A = π(0.40 × 10⁻³)²/4 = 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m². ρ = gradient × A = 4.0 × 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. The 0.30 Ω intercept (contact resistance) does not affect the gradient.

questions.stem: Resistors of 3.0 Ω, 6.0 Ω and 8.0 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance of the combination?
Warmed from 20 °C to 40 °C, a copper wire's resistance rises by about 8%. A germanium sample's resistance falls by about half. In both, the ions vibrate more. What does the germanium result show?

options.text: Germanium's ions vibrate less as it warms, unlike copper's.
Germanium is a semiconductor: far more charge carriers are freed, outweighing the extra collisions.
Copper loses free electrons as it warms, and germanium does not.
Germanium expands more than copper, so its cross-sectional area grows.

questions.explanation: Right. Only a large rise in the number of charge carriers can lower the resistance while collisions increase. It behaves like an NTC thermistor.

questions.stem: Three circuits are each made from an identical cell of negligible internal resistance, a resistor and a lamp. In circuit 1 the three form a single closed loop. Circuit 2 is the same loop with an open switch added. Circuit 3 is the same loop as circuit 1 with a wire of negligible resistance connected directly across the lamp's terminals. Which ranks the currents I₁, I₂ and I₃ in the lamps of circuits 1, 2 and 3?

options.text: I₁ > I₂ = I₃
I₁ = I₃ > I₂
I₃ > I₁ > I₂
I₁ = I₂ = I₃

questions.stem: A cable is made from a ceramic superconductor with a critical temperature of 92 K. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It needs liquid helium (4 K), since every superconductor must be close to absolute zero.
Liquid nitrogen (77 K) keeps it superconducting, so it can carry a current with no heating.
It superconducts at room temperature, since 92 is well above zero.
At 77 K its resistivity is very small but not zero, so it still heats slightly.

questions.explanation: Right. 77 K is below 92 K, so its resistivity is zero: no energy is transferred as heat, however large the current.

questions.stem: Three identical lamps are connected to a supply of negligible internal resistance: lamp A is in series with lamps B and C, which are in parallel with each other. The filament of lamp C breaks. What happens to the brightness of lamps A and B? (Assume each lamp's resistance stays the same.)

options.text: A and B both go out, because the circuit is now broken.
A becomes dimmer and B becomes brighter.
A stays the same and B becomes brighter, because B now carries C's current.
A becomes brighter and B stays the same, because the parallel branch keeps its potential difference.

questions.stem: An unlabelled wire has a mean diameter of 0.32 mm. Its resistance between the clips is 1.72 Ω at a length of 0.20 m and 5.37 Ω at 0.80 m. Resistivities: copper 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m; iron 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m; constantan 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m; nichrome 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m. Which metal is the wire most likely made of?

options.text: Copper
Iron
Constantan
Nichrome

questions.stem: A 9.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance is connected to three resistors in series. The potential differences across two of them are 2.0 V and 4.5 V. What is the potential difference across the third resistor?
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved round the loop: the three potential differences add up to the supply's 9.0 V. 9.0 − 2.0 − 4.5 = 2.5 V.
